item.itunes:summary:

值得閱讀的理由

  • 解析中國大陸年輕人重新閱讀毛澤東著作的現象，避免把它簡化成單純的政治崇拜或網路迷因。
  • 整理「民族主義、成功學、左翼批判、借古諷今」四種不同的毛澤東熱，呈現其背後多元的社會情緒。
  • 探討青年就業、住房與勞動壓力如何讓個人困境被重新理解為結構性問題。
  • 說明「老師」這個稱呼如何透過網路文化，讓歷史政治人物轉化為貼近日常生活的象徵。

摘要

毛澤東為何重新受到年輕人注目

作者觀察到，中國大陸網路上再次出現閱讀《毛澤東選集》、引用《矛盾論》《實踐論》等著作的風潮。有人稱毛澤東為「老師」或「原神」，也有人在影片留言中高呼「人民萬歲」。然而，這不代表年輕人都認同毛澤東時代，更不能直接推論革命理想全面復興；不同群體可能各自取用毛澤東形象與思想中的一部分。

從「主席」到「老師」：歷史人物的網路轉型

「老師」一詞的來源，可追溯至毛澤東在1970年與美國記者埃德加・斯諾的談話。相較於「主席」所代表的國家領袖與政治權威，「老師」顯得親近，彷彿能為年輕人的生活難題提供指點。於是，原本討論革命戰爭與階級鬥爭的著作，被網路重新包裝成面對職場挫折、考試失利或創業受阻時的處世指南。

四種不同的「毛粉」

作者將網路上的毛澤東支持者概括為四類。第一類是民族主義者，欣賞毛澤東建立政權、與美蘇對峙的歷史形象；第二類是成功學取向者，抽取調查研究、抓主要矛盾、集中優勢力量等方法，應用在考試與工作上；第三類是左翼批判者，借用階級、剝削與資本等語言，關注貧富差距、勞工權益及資本壟斷；第四類則是借毛澤東之名批評當下的人，談論過去，實際上指向現今的官僚與權力問題。

個人奮鬥敘事逐漸失去說服力

改革開放以來，社會曾流行一套向上流動的故事：只要努力讀書、找到好工作、肯吃苦，明天就會更好。經濟高速成長時，這套敘事確實曾讓不少人透過教育、創業或房地產改善生活。但如今，學歷貶值、青年就業壓力、房價負擔、工時漫長與薪資成長有限，使許多年輕人開始懷疑，努力是否必然換來更好的未來。字幕提及，當年中國大陸16至24歲、排除在校生的青年失業率曾達17.9%，顯示困境並非只是少數人不夠努力。

以政治語言重新理解個人困境

閱讀毛澤東著作，可能讓人從「我能力不足，所以找不到好工作」，轉而追問「產業結構是否出了問題」；也可能從「我不夠努力，所以薪水太低」，轉而思考勞資權力是否失衡。政治語言因此把原本被視為個人失敗的經驗，重新放回社會結構中理解。作者指出，這種閱讀不必然意味著認同文化大革命等歷史事件，也可能是年輕人用來描述現實不滿的工具。

借古諷今與現實批判

在政治議題難以直接討論、也難以透過正常方式改變的環境裡，毛澤東成為一面特殊的盾牌：批評者引用官方奉為正統的毛澤東思想，追問當權者是否仍反對官僚主義、是否以工人階級為主人、是否真正「為人民服務」。這種借古諷今讓歷史口號轉化為批評當下的語言，也使官方論述與現實之間的落差變得尷尬而顯眼。

影片開頭另有一段商品宣傳，作者介紹以中華民國地圖為主題的周邊商品，並表達以三民主義完成復國建國使命的立場。至於影片主題，作者的核心追問是：當年輕人對現實不滿，卻難以公開談論或改變現實時，為什麼會回頭借用一位已離世半世紀的歷史人物發聲？字幕在作者開始進一步談論年輕人閱讀毛澤東的原因時中斷，未呈現後續論述。

================================================

The most interesting saying in mainland China today is that you can worship Mao Zedong, but you cannot truly emulate him . Isn't Mao Zedong Thought written into the CCP's political orthodoxy by the party itself? Therefore, a very absurd phenomenon has emerged in the mainland today: for some young people criticizing reality, the safest shield is actually Mao Zedong. You cannot directly criticize current leaders, so I will quote Mao to criticize bureaucrats. If you won't let me criticize the collusion of capital and power, then I will use your own revolutionary theories to question you. I ask, didn't you say you. wanted to oppose bureaucracy? Isn't the working class the master of the country ? Didn't you say "long live the people" ? Didn't you say "serve the people"? Suddenly, the situation becomes very awkward; this is essentially a case of " using the past to satirize the present. " People often ask about the map in the background. This map is not just A-Niu's dream of the Republic of China's territory, but also what the 1.4 billion children of China believe the Republic of China should look like. We aim to recover the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to carry out the mission of restoring the Republic and rebuilding the nation. We have launched. a merchandise bundle including the map poster, map tapestry, map pillow, and ROC flag pin. Only children make choices ; I want it all! Take it all home for just 1911. And now, orders over 699 on both platforms qualify for free shipping ! Friends overseas don't need to worry; we will launch an international purchasing plan soon, so get ready to grab yours! Hello everyone, I'm A-Niu. Recently, a friend told me that there is a very interesting, and perhaps even a bit bizarre, phenomenon emerging among young people in mainland China today. That is, Mao Zedong seems to have become popular again. Many young people are starting to re-read the Selected Works. of Mao Zedong, and on Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, and Douyin, you often see people quoting "On Contradiction,""On Practice," and "On Protracted War." Even more interestingly, many young people now don't even call him "Chairman Mao" directly, nor do they use his name, but instead call him "The Original." This makes me very curious. It is already the 21st century. Today's young people in the mainland grew up with smartphones, food delivery, online games, short videos, and AI. Do they really yearn for. that era from 50 or 60 years ago, defined by extreme material scarcity, constant political movements, and where saying one wrong word could change a person's fate? Have the Cultural Revolution, the Great Leap Forward, and the People's Communes all suddenly stopped counting? Or have these young people really suddenly started believing in Mao Zedong again? If we say they are just brainwashed by the CCP, that answer is not entirely wrong, but it is actually too simplistic. Conversely, if someone sees young people reading the. Selected Works of Mao and declares that Chinese youth are reawakening and that revolutionary ideals are reviving, they are likely looking in the completely wrong direction. Because the "Teacher" cult on the Chinese internet today isn't a single political ideology. Some like Mao Zedong's image of a powerful nation in war and diplomacy, some treat his works as a guide to workplace success, some use them to criticize capitalists, and an even more interesting group seemingly praises Mao while actually scolding people who have nothing to do.

with 60 years ago. So, today I don't just want to think about why mainland youth are worshipping Mao Zedong again, but why, when an entire generation is dissatisfied with reality yet unable to discuss politics or change it normally, they end up having to reach back into history and hand a microphone to someone who has been dead for 50 years? Let’s start with the term "Teacher." Where did it come from? A 1970 conversation between Mao Zedong and American journalist Edgar. Snow. It was during the Cultural Revolution, and Mao had a bunch of exaggerated titles—Great Teacher, Great Leader, Great Supreme Commander, Great Helmsman—the "Four Greats." But in the later transcript of that talk , Mao himself expressed that these titles were going too far, saying he had always just been a teacher, so that title could be kept. Decades have passed, and this title has now been reclaimed by mainland youth. But have you noticed that "Chairman" and "Teacher" sound completely different? Chairman Mao is a national leader, a political authority, the man hanging on the Tiananmen Gate, someone very distant . But "Teacher"? It sounds like someone sitting right next to you. It’s as if when you encounter life problems, he would tell you, "Young person, don't panic. First, analyze the primary contradiction, do your research, don't meet things head-on, and learn to fight a protracted war." The entire persona. changes instantly. A 20 th-century revolutionary leader, through the repackaging of internet culture, has become a 21 st-century life coach for the youth. Got scolded by your boss? Read "On Contradiction." Can't pass your civil service exam? Read "On Protracted War." Did your startup fail? "A Single Spark Can Start a Prairie Fire." A book originally discussing revolutionary war and class struggle has somehow turned into a survival guide for mainland youth in the workplace. But don't underestimate this change. Political. figures often regain popularity not through serious theory, but through memes, symbols, wordplay, and titles. The word "Teacher" is a highly successful example of this repackaging. Some might ask, "Hey Aniu, isn't this just a small number of people surfing the web?" It's true that there's a lot of meme culture involved. If you look at Bilibili videos about the Korean War, the Long March, or Mao Zedong’s diplomacy, as soon as the background music kicks in, the screen is flooded. with comments like "Long live the Chairman" or "Long live the people." It feels a lot like fan-girling over historical idols. But saying it's all just a fad wouldn't be entirely accurate either. "Selected Works of Mao Zedong" has indeed re-entered the reading lists of some young people. In the annual data released by the Tsinghua University Library, "Selected Works of Mao Zedong" ranked very high in both 2022 and 2023. However, we must be careful. Borrowing a book doesn't mean the entire university.

has turned Maoist. Just like many families in Taiwan own "The Art of War, " it doesn't mean everyone is preparing to go to battle. So, I believe there are roughly four types of "Mao fans" online today. The first is the Nationalist type ; they love stories of Mao winning the civil war, establishing the CCP regime, and his standoffs against the U.S. and the Soviet Union. For them, Mao Zedong is the symbol of the Chinese people finally standing up. The second is the Success-Oriented type; these people. don't really care about communism at all . They strip away the class struggle and only keep concepts like "principal contradictions,""investigation and research,""concentrating superior forces ," and "protracted warfare," then apply them all to exams, startups, and the workplace. Honestly, that's not much different from "The Art of War." The third type is the Left-Wing Critical group. These people care about wealth gaps, capital monopolies, labor rights, and class rigidity, so they've returned to using language like "working class," "exploitation," and "capital." The fourth group is the most politically. significant, the "Mao-Skin-Wearing" critics. They talk about 60 years ago, but their eyes are fixed on 2026. Why now, though? I think the first reason is that the old narrative of individual struggle from the past few decades has started to lose its appeal. During the rapid growth of the reform and opening-up era, Chinese society had a simple story: "It’s okay if you’re poor now. Study hard, get into a good university, find a job in Beijing, Shanghai, or Guangzhou, work overtime, save up for a house. As long as you’re. willing to endure hardship, tomorrow will definitely be better than today." This story was powerful because, during a period of high economic growth, it actually happened for a lot of people. Children from rural families had the chance to move to the city through education, and ordinary people could change their class status through startups, real estate, or the internet industry, so people were willing to endure because they believed today's hardship was for tomorrow's gain. Yet many young people today are suddenly realizing: I’ve clearly been working so hard, so why does tomorrow not. necessarily seem any better? With more and more people graduating from university, degrees are beginning to depreciate. Youth employment pressure is immense, housing prices remain a heavy burden, work hours are long, and wage growth cannot keep up with the cost of living. In July of this year, the unemployment rate for 16-to-24- year-olds in mainland China, excluding students, even reached 17.9%. Of course , this doesn't mean that all 17.9%of these young people are living miserable lives, but at the very least, it shows that this isn't just a case of a few individuals not trying hard enough. And. this is where the Selected Works of Mao Zedong offer a completely different way of interpretation. Before, you might think, "I can't find a good job because I'm not capable enough." Now, you start to ask, "Isn't there a problem with the industrial structure?" Before, you might think, "My salary is low because I'm not working hard enough." Now, you start to ask, "Is the power dynamic between labor and capital fundamentally lopsided?" This is the power of political language ; it takes what was originally considered a personal failure and reframes it within the social structure . So, many young people read Mao Zedong not necessarily because they truly.

believe the Cultural Revolution was great, but because for the first time, they have found a set of language. A language that tells them perhaps the problem doesn't lie entirely with them, but that the rules of the game in this society are inherently flawed. However, if it were only that, we would misjudge the situation, because the other half of current "Mao Fever" is actually the complete opposite of leftist critique: nationalism. What kind of national narrative have young people in mainland China grown up with today? The great. rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the century of humiliation, China's rise, the East rising while the West declines , and the US containment of China. In this narrative, Mao Zedong is a perfect symbol. He can be portrayed as the one who fought the US, dared to break with the Soviet Union, stood tough against the West, and made China a global power . So, whenever US-China conflicts intensify or the international environment grows tense, this image of Mao Zedong is especially prone to resurfacing. But if you truly cared. about the working class that Mao spoke of, you should be asking about labor conditions; if you truly cared about the people being the masters of the country , you should be asking how much political power the people have. However , the nationalist version of Mao almost never touches on these things; it only talks about whether China is strong enough and whether China is winning. Therefore, behind the same slogan "Long live Chairman Mao," there may be two completely different types of people: one is asking why capitalists can treat workers this way, while the other is asking when China can surpass the United. States. But it is the third reason that I think is the most worth observing. If you write on the Chinese internet today , "I believe China's political system has caused a severe power imbalance," the risk is very high. If you say, "The people should have the right to freely form political parties," that is even more forbidden. And if you try to organize an independent labor union? It would immediately become more than just a post. But what if you changed your approach? Aren't you supposed to be against bureaucracy? Isn't the working class supposed to be the master of the. nation? Isn't "Long live the people" a common slogan? Don't you claim to serve the people? Suddenly, the situation becomes very awkward, because Mao Zedong was the CCP’s own founding leader, and isn't Mao Zedong Thought written into the CCP’s own political orthodoxy? Therefore, a very absurd phenomenon has emerged in China today: for some young people criticizing reality, the safest shield turns out to be Mao Zedong. If you can't ask about the present, then I'll ask about the past. If you can't criticize current leaders directly, then. I'll quote Mao to criticize bureaucracy . If you won't let me criticize the fusion of capital and power, then I'll bring out your own revolutionary theory to question you. This is essentially using the past to criticize the present . In the past, people invoked the Han, Tang, or Ming dynasties; now, some are invoking Mao Zedong. This has led to a very ironic phenomenon: the CCP actually welcomes you to worship Mao, but they want a sanitized version—patriotic, nationalist, anti-American, and visionary, preferably living forever only in memorial halls, textbooks, and.

short videos. It’s fine to browse "Long Live Chairman Mao" on Bilibili, fine to lay flowers at his statue, and fine to read the Selected Works of Mao Zedong at home. But if you actually apply Mao’s political methods—workers organizing themselves, students and workers networking, the masses building political organizations, challenging the bureaucracy, and questioning the relationship between power and capital— well, that’s a different story. That’s why I think the most intriguing saying. in China today is: you can worship Mao, but you can’t actually be a Maoist. The 2018 Jasic incident in Shenzhen made this contradiction very clear. At the time, some workers at Jasic Technology wanted to form a union, and leftist students from universities like Peking University went to support them. These students were not liberals; many truly studied Marx, Lenin, and Mao. Some carried Mao portraits; some sang the Internationale. Workers, students, Marxism, Mao Zedong—according to the. official CCP textbooks, these are all the correct answers. But what was the result? The workers were arrested, the supporters were detained, and Marxist societies in universities were suppressed. Why? Because the issue was never about whether you read Marx; it’s about who gave you permission to organize yourself. Reading the Communist Manifesto in a classroom is fine, but it’s a different story when you actually go out and organize workers. In 2021, delivery rider Chen Guojiang organized the "Meng Shou Hu" network to speak up. for riders, only to face suppression later. The real issue is that the CCP doesn't fear you studying a dead revolution; it fears you learning how to organize from it. Is Mao Zedong really the cure? Some might misunderstand me at this point. " >> Hey, are you saying that since young people in the mainland are unhappy with bureaucratic capitalism and the wealth gap, they should just go back to the Maoist path?" >> Not exactly. I actually think this is the most dangerous part of the whole " Leftist" trend. Because when a society is disillusioned with the present, it’s prone to the mistake of romanticizing a past it never personally lived through. Many young people in China see the young Mao, the crossing of the river, the Long March, the Korean War, and Nixon’s visit , all set to inspiring music. But what’s edited out of these videos? The Anti-Rightist Campaign? The Great Leap Forward? The Great Famine? What about the Cultural Revolution and the countless ordinary people whose lives. were destroyed, humiliated, and persecuted? Those are all missing. Mao did leave behind political rhetoric about opposing privilege and valuing equality. But we cannot forget that the same political system also created a country where there were virtually no institutional checks on the supreme leader. When a leader is always " correct," the media can’t criticize them , the judiciary can’t restrain them, and the people can’t vote them out, then even the noble word "people" can become.

a pretext for disaster. So, if we hope for another unchecked strongman because we're frustrated by bureaucratic capitalism, or if we romanticize tearing down the system with mass movements because current channels for dissent are blocked, that isn't liberation—it’s just using 20 th-century poison to treat 21 st-century ailments. Also, note that youth anxiety isn't unique to China. Taiwan has high housing prices and low wages; South Korea has "Hell Joseon" and the "N-po generation." Young people. everywhere are dissatisfied with corporate dominance, class rigidity, and a lack of future. Don't simplify this by pretending youth in democracies are always happy. Democracy won't drop a house from the sky or guarantee you a high salary. So, what is democracy actually good for? I believe its most important function is providing legitimate tools to use when you are dissatisfied. Unhappy with the government? Vote. Think labor treatment is unfair? Form a union. Think the ruling party is terrible? Support or. even start a new party. Want to criticize the president? Do it publicly . If you think the government broke the law, go through the judicial system. The large-scale protests in South Korea weren't as simple as people hitting the streets and the president stepping down the next day; it was civic mobilization , media investigation, parliamentary impeachment, and judicial processes all working together. This is called institutionalized political venting. The greatest value of democracy isn't the absence of social conflict, but ensuring conflict doesn't require revolution to be solved, so people don't have to wait for a savior or another messiah. So if. someone asks me if it’s terrifying that young people in mainland China are reading Mao's works, I would say I’m not actually that afraid of them reading them. History should be read, and Mao Zedong is a very important figure in modern Chinese history, so he is worth studying. What I find truly tragic is why they have so few political languages to choose from when they want to discuss politics. Can liberalism be organized openly? Can social democracy openly form a political party? Can a truly independent labor union be established? Can the media truly investigate the highest authorities? If these paths are all blocked, what is left for the youth ? What remains is a Mao Zedong that even the CCP cannot openly deny. So, in a way , today’s "Mao Fever" isn't Mao’s victory, but a price paid for political language poverty. When a 21 st-century youth has to run back to the 20th century to find language to express their labor plight, political anxiety, and social dissatisfaction, that in. itself is worth thinking about. And for Sun Yat-sen's perspective, it’s even clearer, since the CCP claims to be the successor to his revolutionary cause. So let’s actually examine it through the Three Principles of the People: Nationalism, Democracy, and Livelihood. Which one is shouted the loudest in the mainland today? Nationalism, of course. National rejuvenation, the rise of a great power, the "century of humiliation "—but I have to ask, is a country becoming strong the same thing as an ordinary young person living well? No.

You can have many aircraft carriers and the world’s second-largest GDP, but if a 25-year-old works 12 hours a day and still can't afford to marry, have children, or buy a home, what does the " rise of a great power" really have to do with their life? That’s why Sun Yat-sen talked about Livelihood—equalization of land rights and regulation of capital. The core behind it is that national development cannot just make a few people rich; ordinary people must have the chance to live a secure life. But even more important than Livelihood is Democracy. Who monitors the government? If the government does something wrong, can the people replace them? Can laborers form their own unions? Can the people stand in the way? Can journalists investigate the leadership? Can ordinary people publicly criticize the President without fear? If the answers are all no , then "people as masters of the country " eventually just means someone else is acting as master for them. True civil rights aren't the government saying "I represent you"; true civil rights are people having the power to tell the government, "You do not represent me, I. want someone else." So in the end, I believe the "Mao fever" in China today isn't really telling us that Mao Zedong has returned, but rather that young people are looking for a language to explain their situation. Some look to nationalism, some to class struggle, some to self-help, and some to Mao, but a truly modern nation shouldn't force people to keep searching for answers in the past. A healthy political system should allow an ordinary person, rather than a great. leader, to change their country. If I am unsatisfied today, I don't need a revolution; I just vote you out. If I think a company is exploiting workers, I don't need to call for a Cultural Revolution; I form a union. If I believe the government is corrupt, I don't need to wait for another Mao; I can let the media investigate, let the legislature oversee, and let the judiciary hold them accountable. That is a truly mature political system. So looking back at " Mao fever," it’s not just simple Mao worship, nor is it a sign that Chinese. youth are turning entirely to the left. It contains nationalism, populism, self-help, youth facing unemployment, and anxiety over class rigidity, as well as those using Mao—whom the CCP cannot deny—to secretly question the CCP today . What’s truly worth understanding isn't why these young people are so foolish to believe in Mao again, but why a 21 st-century youth, in order to express their pain, must run back to the 20th century to borrow the words of a dead. leader? I can understand their dissatisfaction, but understanding doesn't mean we must re-embrace the Mao era. Because what mainland China truly needs today isn't another infallible leader, but a system where people can be their own masters even without one. When ordinary people living in mainland China can freely elect their government , publicly criticize national leaders, form political parties, establish truly independent unions, enjoy freedom of.

press and belief, and speak out—when they can vote a government out if it fails, or hold officials accountable through the judiciary—then Chinese youth won't need to dig a voice out of a historical coffin to speak for them, because they will have their own. And I believe this is what true "people as masters of the country,""the world for the public," and "the people's aspiration" really mean. Striving for a China that truly realizes freedom, democracy, civil rights, and prestige remains our unchanging goal. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 解析中國大陸年輕人重新閱讀毛澤東著作的現象，避免把它簡化成單純的政治崇拜或網路迷因。
  • 整理「民族主義、成功學、左翼批判、借古諷今」四種不同的毛澤東熱，呈現其背後多元的社會情緒。
  • 探討青年就業、住房與勞動壓力如何讓個人困境被重新理解為結構性問題。
  • 說明「老師」這個稱呼如何透過網路文化，讓歷史政治人物轉化為貼近日常生活的象徵。

摘要

毛澤東為何重新受到年輕人注目

作者觀察到，中國大陸網路上再次出現閱讀《毛澤東選集》、引用《矛盾論》《實踐論》等著作的風潮。有人稱毛澤東為「老師」或「原神」，也有人在影片留言中高呼「人民萬歲」。然而，這不代表年輕人都認同毛澤東時代，更不能直接推論革命理想全面復興；不同群體可能各自取用毛澤東形象與思想中的一部分。

從「主席」到「老師」：歷史人物的網路轉型

「老師」一詞的來源，可追溯至毛澤東在1970年與美國記者埃德加・斯諾的談話。相較於「主席」所代表的國家領袖與政治權威，「老師」顯得親近，彷彿能為年輕人的生活難題提供指點。於是，原本討論革命戰爭與階級鬥爭的著作，被網路重新包裝成面對職場挫折、考試失利或創業受阻時的處世指南。

四種不同的「毛粉」

作者將網路上的毛澤東支持者概括為四類。第一類是民族主義者，欣賞毛澤東建立政權、與美蘇對峙的歷史形象；第二類是成功學取向者，抽取調查研究、抓主要矛盾、集中優勢力量等方法，應用在考試與工作上；第三類是左翼批判者，借用階級、剝削與資本等語言，關注貧富差距、勞工權益及資本壟斷；第四類則是借毛澤東之名批評當下的人，談論過去，實際上指向現今的官僚與權力問題。

個人奮鬥敘事逐漸失去說服力

改革開放以來，社會曾流行一套向上流動的故事：只要努力讀書、找到好工作、肯吃苦，明天就會更好。經濟高速成長時，這套敘事確實曾讓不少人透過教育、創業或房地產改善生活。但如今，學歷貶值、青年就業壓力、房價負擔、工時漫長與薪資成長有限，使許多年輕人開始懷疑，努力是否必然換來更好的未來。字幕提及，當年中國大陸16至24歲、排除在校生的青年失業率曾達17.9%，顯示困境並非只是少數人不夠努力。

以政治語言重新理解個人困境

閱讀毛澤東著作，可能讓人從「我能力不足，所以找不到好工作」，轉而追問「產業結構是否出了問題」；也可能從「我不夠努力，所以薪水太低」，轉而思考勞資權力是否失衡。政治語言因此把原本被視為個人失敗的經驗，重新放回社會結構中理解。作者指出，這種閱讀不必然意味著認同文化大革命等歷史事件，也可能是年輕人用來描述現實不滿的工具。

借古諷今與現實批判

在政治議題難以直接討論、也難以透過正常方式改變的環境裡，毛澤東成為一面特殊的盾牌：批評者引用官方奉為正統的毛澤東思想，追問當權者是否仍反對官僚主義、是否以工人階級為主人、是否真正「為人民服務」。這種借古諷今讓歷史口號轉化為批評當下的語言，也使官方論述與現實之間的落差變得尷尬而顯眼。

影片開頭另有一段商品宣傳，作者介紹以中華民國地圖為主題的周邊商品，並表達以三民主義完成復國建國使命的立場。至於影片主題，作者的核心追問是：當年輕人對現實不滿，卻難以公開談論或改變現實時，為什麼會回頭借用一位已離世半世紀的歷史人物發聲？字幕在作者開始進一步談論年輕人閱讀毛澤東的原因時中斷，未呈現後續論述。

================================================

The most interesting saying in mainland China today is that you can worship Mao Zedong, but you cannot truly emulate him . Isn't Mao Zedong Thought written into the CCP's political orthodoxy by the party itself? Therefore, a very absurd phenomenon has emerged in the mainland today: for some young people criticizing reality, the safest shield is actually Mao Zedong. You cannot directly criticize current leaders, so I will quote Mao to criticize bureaucrats. If you won't let me criticize the collusion of capital and power, then I will use your own revolutionary theories to question you. I ask, didn't you say you. wanted to oppose bureaucracy? Isn't the working class the master of the country ? Didn't you say "long live the people" ? Didn't you say "serve the people"? Suddenly, the situation becomes very awkward; this is essentially a case of " using the past to satirize the present. " People often ask about the map in the background. This map is not just A-Niu's dream of the Republic of China's territory, but also what the 1.4 billion children of China believe the Republic of China should look like. We aim to recover the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to carry out the mission of restoring the Republic and rebuilding the nation. We have launched. a merchandise bundle including the map poster, map tapestry, map pillow, and ROC flag pin. Only children make choices ; I want it all! Take it all home for just 1911. And now, orders over 699 on both platforms qualify for free shipping ! Friends overseas don't need to worry; we will launch an international purchasing plan soon, so get ready to grab yours! Hello everyone, I'm A-Niu. Recently, a friend told me that there is a very interesting, and perhaps even a bit bizarre, phenomenon emerging among young people in mainland China today. That is, Mao Zedong seems to have become popular again. Many young people are starting to re-read the Selected Works. of Mao Zedong, and on Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, and Douyin, you often see people quoting "On Contradiction,""On Practice," and "On Protracted War." Even more interestingly, many young people now don't even call him "Chairman Mao" directly, nor do they use his name, but instead call him "The Original." This makes me very curious. It is already the 21st century. Today's young people in the mainland grew up with smartphones, food delivery, online games, short videos, and AI. Do they really yearn for. that era from 50 or 60 years ago, defined by extreme material scarcity, constant political movements, and where saying one wrong word could change a person's fate? Have the Cultural Revolution, the Great Leap Forward, and the People's Communes all suddenly stopped counting? Or have these young people really suddenly started believing in Mao Zedong again? If we say they are just brainwashed by the CCP, that answer is not entirely wrong, but it is actually too simplistic. Conversely, if someone sees young people reading the. Selected Works of Mao and declares that Chinese youth are reawakening and that revolutionary ideals are reviving, they are likely looking in the completely wrong direction. Because the "Teacher" cult on the Chinese internet today isn't a single political ideology. Some like Mao Zedong's image of a powerful nation in war and diplomacy, some treat his works as a guide to workplace success, some use them to criticize capitalists, and an even more interesting group seemingly praises Mao while actually scolding people who have nothing to do.

with 60 years ago. So, today I don't just want to think about why mainland youth are worshipping Mao Zedong again, but why, when an entire generation is dissatisfied with reality yet unable to discuss politics or change it normally, they end up having to reach back into history and hand a microphone to someone who has been dead for 50 years? Let’s start with the term "Teacher." Where did it come from? A 1970 conversation between Mao Zedong and American journalist Edgar. Snow. It was during the Cultural Revolution, and Mao had a bunch of exaggerated titles—Great Teacher, Great Leader, Great Supreme Commander, Great Helmsman—the "Four Greats." But in the later transcript of that talk , Mao himself expressed that these titles were going too far, saying he had always just been a teacher, so that title could be kept. Decades have passed, and this title has now been reclaimed by mainland youth. But have you noticed that "Chairman" and "Teacher" sound completely different? Chairman Mao is a national leader, a political authority, the man hanging on the Tiananmen Gate, someone very distant . But "Teacher"? It sounds like someone sitting right next to you. It’s as if when you encounter life problems, he would tell you, "Young person, don't panic. First, analyze the primary contradiction, do your research, don't meet things head-on, and learn to fight a protracted war." The entire persona. changes instantly. A 20 th-century revolutionary leader, through the repackaging of internet culture, has become a 21 st-century life coach for the youth. Got scolded by your boss? Read "On Contradiction." Can't pass your civil service exam? Read "On Protracted War." Did your startup fail? "A Single Spark Can Start a Prairie Fire." A book originally discussing revolutionary war and class struggle has somehow turned into a survival guide for mainland youth in the workplace. But don't underestimate this change. Political. figures often regain popularity not through serious theory, but through memes, symbols, wordplay, and titles. The word "Teacher" is a highly successful example of this repackaging. Some might ask, "Hey Aniu, isn't this just a small number of people surfing the web?" It's true that there's a lot of meme culture involved. If you look at Bilibili videos about the Korean War, the Long March, or Mao Zedong’s diplomacy, as soon as the background music kicks in, the screen is flooded. with comments like "Long live the Chairman" or "Long live the people." It feels a lot like fan-girling over historical idols. But saying it's all just a fad wouldn't be entirely accurate either. "Selected Works of Mao Zedong" has indeed re-entered the reading lists of some young people. In the annual data released by the Tsinghua University Library, "Selected Works of Mao Zedong" ranked very high in both 2022 and 2023. However, we must be careful. Borrowing a book doesn't mean the entire university.

has turned Maoist. Just like many families in Taiwan own "The Art of War, " it doesn't mean everyone is preparing to go to battle. So, I believe there are roughly four types of "Mao fans" online today. The first is the Nationalist type ; they love stories of Mao winning the civil war, establishing the CCP regime, and his standoffs against the U.S. and the Soviet Union. For them, Mao Zedong is the symbol of the Chinese people finally standing up. The second is the Success-Oriented type; these people. don't really care about communism at all . They strip away the class struggle and only keep concepts like "principal contradictions,""investigation and research,""concentrating superior forces ," and "protracted warfare," then apply them all to exams, startups, and the workplace. Honestly, that's not much different from "The Art of War." The third type is the Left-Wing Critical group. These people care about wealth gaps, capital monopolies, labor rights, and class rigidity, so they've returned to using language like "working class," "exploitation," and "capital." The fourth group is the most politically. significant, the "Mao-Skin-Wearing" critics. They talk about 60 years ago, but their eyes are fixed on 2026. Why now, though? I think the first reason is that the old narrative of individual struggle from the past few decades has started to lose its appeal. During the rapid growth of the reform and opening-up era, Chinese society had a simple story: "It’s okay if you’re poor now. Study hard, get into a good university, find a job in Beijing, Shanghai, or Guangzhou, work overtime, save up for a house. As long as you’re. willing to endure hardship, tomorrow will definitely be better than today." This story was powerful because, during a period of high economic growth, it actually happened for a lot of people. Children from rural families had the chance to move to the city through education, and ordinary people could change their class status through startups, real estate, or the internet industry, so people were willing to endure because they believed today's hardship was for tomorrow's gain. Yet many young people today are suddenly realizing: I’ve clearly been working so hard, so why does tomorrow not. necessarily seem any better? With more and more people graduating from university, degrees are beginning to depreciate. Youth employment pressure is immense, housing prices remain a heavy burden, work hours are long, and wage growth cannot keep up with the cost of living. In July of this year, the unemployment rate for 16-to-24- year-olds in mainland China, excluding students, even reached 17.9%. Of course , this doesn't mean that all 17.9%of these young people are living miserable lives, but at the very least, it shows that this isn't just a case of a few individuals not trying hard enough. And. this is where the Selected Works of Mao Zedong offer a completely different way of interpretation. Before, you might think, "I can't find a good job because I'm not capable enough." Now, you start to ask, "Isn't there a problem with the industrial structure?" Before, you might think, "My salary is low because I'm not working hard enough." Now, you start to ask, "Is the power dynamic between labor and capital fundamentally lopsided?" This is the power of political language ; it takes what was originally considered a personal failure and reframes it within the social structure . So, many young people read Mao Zedong not necessarily because they truly.

believe the Cultural Revolution was great, but because for the first time, they have found a set of language. A language that tells them perhaps the problem doesn't lie entirely with them, but that the rules of the game in this society are inherently flawed. However, if it were only that, we would misjudge the situation, because the other half of current "Mao Fever" is actually the complete opposite of leftist critique: nationalism. What kind of national narrative have young people in mainland China grown up with today? The great. rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the century of humiliation, China's rise, the East rising while the West declines , and the US containment of China. In this narrative, Mao Zedong is a perfect symbol. He can be portrayed as the one who fought the US, dared to break with the Soviet Union, stood tough against the West, and made China a global power . So, whenever US-China conflicts intensify or the international environment grows tense, this image of Mao Zedong is especially prone to resurfacing. But if you truly cared. about the working class that Mao spoke of, you should be asking about labor conditions; if you truly cared about the people being the masters of the country , you should be asking how much political power the people have. However , the nationalist version of Mao almost never touches on these things; it only talks about whether China is strong enough and whether China is winning. Therefore, behind the same slogan "Long live Chairman Mao," there may be two completely different types of people: one is asking why capitalists can treat workers this way, while the other is asking when China can surpass the United. States. But it is the third reason that I think is the most worth observing. If you write on the Chinese internet today , "I believe China's political system has caused a severe power imbalance," the risk is very high. If you say, "The people should have the right to freely form political parties," that is even more forbidden. And if you try to organize an independent labor union? It would immediately become more than just a post. But what if you changed your approach? Aren't you supposed to be against bureaucracy? Isn't the working class supposed to be the master of the. nation? Isn't "Long live the people" a common slogan? Don't you claim to serve the people? Suddenly, the situation becomes very awkward, because Mao Zedong was the CCP’s own founding leader, and isn't Mao Zedong Thought written into the CCP’s own political orthodoxy? Therefore, a very absurd phenomenon has emerged in China today: for some young people criticizing reality, the safest shield turns out to be Mao Zedong. If you can't ask about the present, then I'll ask about the past. If you can't criticize current leaders directly, then. I'll quote Mao to criticize bureaucracy . If you won't let me criticize the fusion of capital and power, then I'll bring out your own revolutionary theory to question you. This is essentially using the past to criticize the present . In the past, people invoked the Han, Tang, or Ming dynasties; now, some are invoking Mao Zedong. This has led to a very ironic phenomenon: the CCP actually welcomes you to worship Mao, but they want a sanitized version—patriotic, nationalist, anti-American, and visionary, preferably living forever only in memorial halls, textbooks, and.

short videos. It’s fine to browse "Long Live Chairman Mao" on Bilibili, fine to lay flowers at his statue, and fine to read the Selected Works of Mao Zedong at home. But if you actually apply Mao’s political methods—workers organizing themselves, students and workers networking, the masses building political organizations, challenging the bureaucracy, and questioning the relationship between power and capital— well, that’s a different story. That’s why I think the most intriguing saying. in China today is: you can worship Mao, but you can’t actually be a Maoist. The 2018 Jasic incident in Shenzhen made this contradiction very clear. At the time, some workers at Jasic Technology wanted to form a union, and leftist students from universities like Peking University went to support them. These students were not liberals; many truly studied Marx, Lenin, and Mao. Some carried Mao portraits; some sang the Internationale. Workers, students, Marxism, Mao Zedong—according to the. official CCP textbooks, these are all the correct answers. But what was the result? The workers were arrested, the supporters were detained, and Marxist societies in universities were suppressed. Why? Because the issue was never about whether you read Marx; it’s about who gave you permission to organize yourself. Reading the Communist Manifesto in a classroom is fine, but it’s a different story when you actually go out and organize workers. In 2021, delivery rider Chen Guojiang organized the "Meng Shou Hu" network to speak up. for riders, only to face suppression later. The real issue is that the CCP doesn't fear you studying a dead revolution; it fears you learning how to organize from it. Is Mao Zedong really the cure? Some might misunderstand me at this point. " >> Hey, are you saying that since young people in the mainland are unhappy with bureaucratic capitalism and the wealth gap, they should just go back to the Maoist path?" >> Not exactly. I actually think this is the most dangerous part of the whole " Leftist" trend. Because when a society is disillusioned with the present, it’s prone to the mistake of romanticizing a past it never personally lived through. Many young people in China see the young Mao, the crossing of the river, the Long March, the Korean War, and Nixon’s visit , all set to inspiring music. But what’s edited out of these videos? The Anti-Rightist Campaign? The Great Leap Forward? The Great Famine? What about the Cultural Revolution and the countless ordinary people whose lives. were destroyed, humiliated, and persecuted? Those are all missing. Mao did leave behind political rhetoric about opposing privilege and valuing equality. But we cannot forget that the same political system also created a country where there were virtually no institutional checks on the supreme leader. When a leader is always " correct," the media can’t criticize them , the judiciary can’t restrain them, and the people can’t vote them out, then even the noble word "people" can become.

a pretext for disaster. So, if we hope for another unchecked strongman because we're frustrated by bureaucratic capitalism, or if we romanticize tearing down the system with mass movements because current channels for dissent are blocked, that isn't liberation—it’s just using 20 th-century poison to treat 21 st-century ailments. Also, note that youth anxiety isn't unique to China. Taiwan has high housing prices and low wages; South Korea has "Hell Joseon" and the "N-po generation." Young people. everywhere are dissatisfied with corporate dominance, class rigidity, and a lack of future. Don't simplify this by pretending youth in democracies are always happy. Democracy won't drop a house from the sky or guarantee you a high salary. So, what is democracy actually good for? I believe its most important function is providing legitimate tools to use when you are dissatisfied. Unhappy with the government? Vote. Think labor treatment is unfair? Form a union. Think the ruling party is terrible? Support or. even start a new party. Want to criticize the president? Do it publicly . If you think the government broke the law, go through the judicial system. The large-scale protests in South Korea weren't as simple as people hitting the streets and the president stepping down the next day; it was civic mobilization , media investigation, parliamentary impeachment, and judicial processes all working together. This is called institutionalized political venting. The greatest value of democracy isn't the absence of social conflict, but ensuring conflict doesn't require revolution to be solved, so people don't have to wait for a savior or another messiah. So if. someone asks me if it’s terrifying that young people in mainland China are reading Mao's works, I would say I’m not actually that afraid of them reading them. History should be read, and Mao Zedong is a very important figure in modern Chinese history, so he is worth studying. What I find truly tragic is why they have so few political languages to choose from when they want to discuss politics. Can liberalism be organized openly? Can social democracy openly form a political party? Can a truly independent labor union be established? Can the media truly investigate the highest authorities? If these paths are all blocked, what is left for the youth ? What remains is a Mao Zedong that even the CCP cannot openly deny. So, in a way , today’s "Mao Fever" isn't Mao’s victory, but a price paid for political language poverty. When a 21 st-century youth has to run back to the 20th century to find language to express their labor plight, political anxiety, and social dissatisfaction, that in. itself is worth thinking about. And for Sun Yat-sen's perspective, it’s even clearer, since the CCP claims to be the successor to his revolutionary cause. So let’s actually examine it through the Three Principles of the People: Nationalism, Democracy, and Livelihood. Which one is shouted the loudest in the mainland today? Nationalism, of course. National rejuvenation, the rise of a great power, the "century of humiliation "—but I have to ask, is a country becoming strong the same thing as an ordinary young person living well? No.

You can have many aircraft carriers and the world’s second-largest GDP, but if a 25-year-old works 12 hours a day and still can't afford to marry, have children, or buy a home, what does the " rise of a great power" really have to do with their life? That’s why Sun Yat-sen talked about Livelihood—equalization of land rights and regulation of capital. The core behind it is that national development cannot just make a few people rich; ordinary people must have the chance to live a secure life. But even more important than Livelihood is Democracy. Who monitors the government? If the government does something wrong, can the people replace them? Can laborers form their own unions? Can the people stand in the way? Can journalists investigate the leadership? Can ordinary people publicly criticize the President without fear? If the answers are all no , then "people as masters of the country " eventually just means someone else is acting as master for them. True civil rights aren't the government saying "I represent you"; true civil rights are people having the power to tell the government, "You do not represent me, I. want someone else." So in the end, I believe the "Mao fever" in China today isn't really telling us that Mao Zedong has returned, but rather that young people are looking for a language to explain their situation. Some look to nationalism, some to class struggle, some to self-help, and some to Mao, but a truly modern nation shouldn't force people to keep searching for answers in the past. A healthy political system should allow an ordinary person, rather than a great. leader, to change their country. If I am unsatisfied today, I don't need a revolution; I just vote you out. If I think a company is exploiting workers, I don't need to call for a Cultural Revolution; I form a union. If I believe the government is corrupt, I don't need to wait for another Mao; I can let the media investigate, let the legislature oversee, and let the judiciary hold them accountable. That is a truly mature political system. So looking back at " Mao fever," it’s not just simple Mao worship, nor is it a sign that Chinese. youth are turning entirely to the left. It contains nationalism, populism, self-help, youth facing unemployment, and anxiety over class rigidity, as well as those using Mao—whom the CCP cannot deny—to secretly question the CCP today . What’s truly worth understanding isn't why these young people are so foolish to believe in Mao again, but why a 21 st-century youth, in order to express their pain, must run back to the 20th century to borrow the words of a dead. leader? I can understand their dissatisfaction, but understanding doesn't mean we must re-embrace the Mao era. Because what mainland China truly needs today isn't another infallible leader, but a system where people can be their own masters even without one. When ordinary people living in mainland China can freely elect their government , publicly criticize national leaders, form political parties, establish truly independent unions, enjoy freedom of.

press and belief, and speak out—when they can vote a government out if it fails, or hold officials accountable through the judiciary—then Chinese youth won't need to dig a voice out of a historical coffin to speak for them, because they will have their own. And I believe this is what true "people as masters of the country,""the world for the public," and "the people's aspiration" really mean. Striving for a China that truly realizes freedom, democracy, civil rights, and prestige remains our unchanging goal. The. politics of the National Revolution may face a hundred setbacks, but they will never end. Alright, that’s all for today’s story. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 解析中國大陸年輕人重新閱讀毛澤東著作的現象，避免把它簡化成單純的政治崇拜或網路迷因。
  • 整理「民族主義、成功學、左翼批判、借古諷今」四種不同的毛澤東熱，呈現其背後多元的社會情緒。
  • 探討青年就業、住房與勞動壓力如何讓個人困境被重新理解為結構性問題。
  • 說明「老師」這個稱呼如何透過網路文化，讓歷史政治人物轉化為貼近日常生活的象徵。

摘要

毛澤東為何重新受到年輕人注目

作者觀察到，中國大陸網路上再次出現閱讀《毛澤東選集》、引用《矛盾論》《實踐論》等著作的風潮。有人稱毛澤東為「老師」或「原神」，也有人在影片留言中高呼「人民萬歲」。然而，這不代表年輕人都認同毛澤東時代，更不能直接推論革命理想全面復興；不同群體可能各自取用毛澤東形象與思想中的一部分。

從「主席」到「老師」：歷史人物的網路轉型

「老師」一詞的來源，可追溯至毛澤東在1970年與美國記者埃德加・斯諾的談話。相較於「主席」所代表的國家領袖與政治權威，「老師」顯得親近，彷彿能為年輕人的生活難題提供指點。於是，原本討論革命戰爭與階級鬥爭的著作，被網路重新包裝成面對職場挫折、考試失利或創業受阻時的處世指南。

四種不同的「毛粉」

作者將網路上的毛澤東支持者概括為四類。第一類是民族主義者，欣賞毛澤東建立政權、與美蘇對峙的歷史形象；第二類是成功學取向者，抽取調查研究、抓主要矛盾、集中優勢力量等方法，應用在考試與工作上；第三類是左翼批判者，借用階級、剝削與資本等語言，關注貧富差距、勞工權益及資本壟斷；第四類則是借毛澤東之名批評當下的人，談論過去，實際上指向現今的官僚與權力問題。

個人奮鬥敘事逐漸失去說服力

改革開放以來，社會曾流行一套向上流動的故事：只要努力讀書、找到好工作、肯吃苦，明天就會更好。經濟高速成長時，這套敘事確實曾讓不少人透過教育、創業或房地產改善生活。但如今，學歷貶值、青年就業壓力、房價負擔、工時漫長與薪資成長有限，使許多年輕人開始懷疑，努力是否必然換來更好的未來。字幕提及，當年中國大陸16至24歲、排除在校生的青年失業率曾達17.9%，顯示困境並非只是少數人不夠努力。

以政治語言重新理解個人困境

閱讀毛澤東著作，可能讓人從「我能力不足，所以找不到好工作」，轉而追問「產業結構是否出了問題」；也可能從「我不夠努力，所以薪水太低」，轉而思考勞資權力是否失衡。政治語言因此把原本被視為個人失敗的經驗，重新放回社會結構中理解。作者指出，這種閱讀不必然意味著認同文化大革命等歷史事件，也可能是年輕人用來描述現實不滿的工具。

借古諷今與現實批判

在政治議題難以直接討論、也難以透過正常方式改變的環境裡，毛澤東成為一面特殊的盾牌：批評者引用官方奉為正統的毛澤東思想，追問當權者是否仍反對官僚主義、是否以工人階級為主人、是否真正「為人民服務」。這種借古諷今讓歷史口號轉化為批評當下的語言，也使官方論述與現實之間的落差變得尷尬而顯眼。

影片開頭另有一段商品宣傳，作者介紹以中華民國地圖為主題的周邊商品，並表達以三民主義完成復國建國使命的立場。至於影片主題，作者的核心追問是：當年輕人對現實不滿，卻難以公開談論或改變現實時，為什麼會回頭借用一位已離世半世紀的歷史人物發聲？字幕在作者開始進一步談論年輕人閱讀毛澤東的原因時中斷，未呈現後續論述。

================================================

The most interesting saying in mainland China today is that you can worship Mao Zedong, but you cannot truly emulate him . Isn't Mao Zedong Thought written into the CCP's political orthodoxy by the party itself? Therefore, a very absurd phenomenon has emerged in the mainland today: for some young people criticizing reality, the safest shield is actually Mao Zedong. You cannot directly criticize current leaders, so I will quote Mao to criticize bureaucrats. If you won't let me criticize the collusion of capital and power, then I will use your own revolutionary theories to question you. I ask, didn't you say you. wanted to oppose bureaucracy? Isn't the working class the master of the country ? Didn't you say "long live the people" ? Didn't you say "serve the people"? Suddenly, the situation becomes very awkward; this is essentially a case of " using the past to satirize the present. " People often ask about the map in the background. This map is not just A-Niu's dream of the Republic of China's territory, but also what the 1.4 billion children of China believe the Republic of China should look like. We aim to recover the Republic of China, using the Three Principles of the People from the National Revolution to carry out the mission of restoring the Republic and rebuilding the nation. We have launched. a merchandise bundle including the map poster, map tapestry, map pillow, and ROC flag pin. Only children make choices ; I want it all! Take it all home for just 1911. And now, orders over 699 on both platforms qualify for free shipping ! Friends overseas don't need to worry; we will launch an international purchasing plan soon, so get ready to grab yours! Hello everyone, I'm A-Niu. Recently, a friend told me that there is a very interesting, and perhaps even a bit bizarre, phenomenon emerging among young people in mainland China today. That is, Mao Zedong seems to have become popular again. Many young people are starting to re-read the Selected Works. of Mao Zedong, and on Bilibili, Xiaohongshu, and Douyin, you often see people quoting "On Contradiction,""On Practice," and "On Protracted War." Even more interestingly, many young people now don't even call him "Chairman Mao" directly, nor do they use his name, but instead call him "The Original." This makes me very curious. It is already the 21st century. Today's young people in the mainland grew up with smartphones, food delivery, online games, short videos, and AI. Do they really yearn for. that era from 50 or 60 years ago, defined by extreme material scarcity, constant political movements, and where saying one wrong word could change a person's fate? Have the Cultural Revolution, the Great Leap Forward, and the People's Communes all suddenly stopped counting? Or have these young people really suddenly started believing in Mao Zedong again? If we say they are just brainwashed by the CCP, that answer is not entirely wrong, but it is actually too simplistic. Conversely, if someone sees young people reading the. Selected Works of Mao and declares that Chinese youth are reawakening and that revolutionary ideals are reviving, they are likely looking in the completely wrong direction. Because the "Teacher" cult on the Chinese internet today isn't a single political ideology. Some like Mao Zedong's image of a powerful nation in war and diplomacy, some treat his works as a guide to workplace success, some use them to criticize capitalists, and an even more interesting group seemingly praises Mao while actually scolding people who have nothing to do.

with 60 years ago. So, today I don't just want to think about why mainland youth are worshipping Mao Zedong again, but why, when an entire generation is dissatisfied with reality yet unable to discuss politics or change it normally, they end up having to reach back into history and hand a microphone to someone who has been dead for 50 years? Let’s start with the term "Teacher." Where did it come from? A 1970 conversation between Mao Zedong and American journalist Edgar. Snow. It was during the Cultural Revolution, and Mao had a bunch of exaggerated titles—Great Teacher, Great Leader, Great Supreme Commander, Great Helmsman—the "Four Greats." But in the later transcript of that talk , Mao himself expressed that these titles were going too far, saying he had always just been a teacher, so that title could be kept. Decades have passed, and this title has now been reclaimed by mainland youth. But have you noticed that "Chairman" and "Teacher" sound completely different? Chairman Mao is a national leader, a political authority, the man hanging on the Tiananmen Gate, someone very distant . But "Teacher"? It sounds like someone sitting right next to you. It’s as if when you encounter life problems, he would tell you, "Young person, don't panic. First, analyze the primary contradiction, do your research, don't meet things head-on, and learn to fight a protracted war." The entire persona. changes instantly. A 20 th-century revolutionary leader, through the repackaging of internet culture, has become a 21 st-century life coach for the youth. Got scolded by your boss? Read "On Contradiction." Can't pass your civil service exam? Read "On Protracted War." Did your startup fail? "A Single Spark Can Start a Prairie Fire." A book originally discussing revolutionary war and class struggle has somehow turned into a survival guide for mainland youth in the workplace. But don't underestimate this change. Political. figures often regain popularity not through serious theory, but through memes, symbols, wordplay, and titles. The word "Teacher" is a highly successful example of this repackaging. Some might ask, "Hey Aniu, isn't this just a small number of people surfing the web?" It's true that there's a lot of meme culture involved. If you look at Bilibili videos about the Korean War, the Long March, or Mao Zedong’s diplomacy, as soon as the background music kicks in, the screen is flooded. with comments like "Long live the Chairman" or "Long live the people." It feels a lot like fan-girling over historical idols. But saying it's all just a fad wouldn't be entirely accurate either. "Selected Works of Mao Zedong" has indeed re-entered the reading lists of some young people. In the annual data released by the Tsinghua University Library, "Selected Works of Mao Zedong" ranked very high in both 2022 and 2023. However, we must be careful. Borrowing a book doesn't mean the entire university.

has turned Maoist. Just like many families in Taiwan own "The Art of War, " it doesn't mean everyone is preparing to go to battle. So, I believe there are roughly four types of "Mao fans" online today. The first is the Nationalist type ; they love stories of Mao winning the civil war, establishing the CCP regime, and his standoffs against the U.S. and the Soviet Union. For them, Mao Zedong is the symbol of the Chinese people finally standing up. The second is the Success-Oriented type; these people. don't really care about communism at all . They strip away the class struggle and only keep concepts like "principal contradictions,""investigation and research,""concentrating superior forces ," and "protracted warfare," then apply them all to exams, startups, and the workplace. Honestly, that's not much different from "The Art of War." The third type is the Left-Wing Critical group. These people care about wealth gaps, capital monopolies, labor rights, and class rigidity, so they've returned to using language like "working class," "exploitation," and "capital." The fourth group is the most politically. significant, the "Mao-Skin-Wearing" critics. They talk about 60 years ago, but their eyes are fixed on 2026. Why now, though? I think the first reason is that the old narrative of individual struggle from the past few decades has started to lose its appeal. During the rapid growth of the reform and opening-up era, Chinese society had a simple story: "It’s okay if you’re poor now. Study hard, get into a good university, find a job in Beijing, Shanghai, or Guangzhou, work overtime, save up for a house. As long as you’re. willing to endure hardship, tomorrow will definitely be better than today." This story was powerful because, during a period of high economic growth, it actually happened for a lot of people. Children from rural families had the chance to move to the city through education, and ordinary people could change their class status through startups, real estate, or the internet industry, so people were willing to endure because they believed today's hardship was for tomorrow's gain. Yet many young people today are suddenly realizing: I’ve clearly been working so hard, so why does tomorrow not. necessarily seem any better? With more and more people graduating from university, degrees are beginning to depreciate. Youth employment pressure is immense, housing prices remain a heavy burden, work hours are long, and wage growth cannot keep up with the cost of living. In July of this year, the unemployment rate for 16-to-24- year-olds in mainland China, excluding students, even reached 17.9%. Of course , this doesn't mean that all 17.9%of these young people are living miserable lives, but at the very least, it shows that this isn't just a case of a few individuals not trying hard enough. And. this is where the Selected Works of Mao Zedong offer a completely different way of interpretation. Before, you might think, "I can't find a good job because I'm not capable enough." Now, you start to ask, "Isn't there a problem with the industrial structure?" Before, you might think, "My salary is low because I'm not working hard enough." Now, you start to ask, "Is the power dynamic between labor and capital fundamentally lopsided?" This is the power of political language ; it takes what was originally considered a personal failure and reframes it within the social structure . So, many young people read Mao Zedong not necessarily because they truly.

believe the Cultural Revolution was great, but because for the first time, they have found a set of language. A language that tells them perhaps the problem doesn't lie entirely with them, but that the rules of the game in this society are inherently flawed. However, if it were only that, we would misjudge the situation, because the other half of current "Mao Fever" is actually the complete opposite of leftist critique: nationalism. What kind of national narrative have young people in mainland China grown up with today? The great. rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, the century of humiliation, China's rise, the East rising while the West declines , and the US containment of China. In this narrative, Mao Zedong is a perfect symbol. He can be portrayed as the one who fought the US, dared to break with the Soviet Union, stood tough against the West, and made China a global power . So, whenever US-China conflicts intensify or the international environment grows tense, this image of Mao Zedong is especially prone to resurfacing. But if you truly cared. about the working class that Mao spoke of, you should be asking about labor conditions; if you truly cared about the people being the masters of the country , you should be asking how much political power the people have. However , the nationalist version of Mao almost never touches on these things; it only talks about whether China is strong enough and whether China is winning. Therefore, behind the same slogan "Long live Chairman Mao," there may be two completely different types of people: one is asking why capitalists can treat workers this way, while the other is asking when China can surpass the United. States. But it is the third reason that I think is the most worth observing. If you write on the Chinese internet today , "I believe China's political system has caused a severe power imbalance," the risk is very high. If you say, "The people should have the right to freely form political parties," that is even more forbidden. And if you try to organize an independent labor union? It would immediately become more than just a post. But what if you changed your approach? Aren't you supposed to be against bureaucracy? Isn't the working class supposed to be the master of the. nation? Isn't "Long live the people" a common slogan? Don't you claim to serve the people? Suddenly, the situation becomes very awkward, because Mao Zedong was the CCP’s own founding leader, and isn't Mao Zedong Thought written into the CCP’s own political orthodoxy? Therefore, a very absurd phenomenon has emerged in China today: for some young people criticizing reality, the safest shield turns out to be Mao Zedong. If you can't ask about the present, then I'll ask about the past. If you can't criticize current leaders directly, then. I'll quote Mao to criticize bureaucracy . If you won't let me criticize the fusion of capital and power, then I'll bring out your own revolutionary theory to question you. This is essentially using the past to criticize the present . In the past, people invoked the Han, Tang, or Ming dynasties; now, some are invoking Mao Zedong. This has led to a very ironic phenomenon: the CCP actually welcomes you to worship Mao, but they want a sanitized version—patriotic, nationalist, anti-American, and visionary, preferably living forever only in memorial halls, textbooks, and.

short videos. It’s fine to browse "Long Live Chairman Mao" on Bilibili, fine to lay flowers at his statue, and fine to read the Selected Works of Mao Zedong at home. But if you actually apply Mao’s political methods—workers organizing themselves, students and workers networking, the masses building political organizations, challenging the bureaucracy, and questioning the relationship between power and capital— well, that’s a different story. That’s why I think the most intriguing saying. in China today is: you can worship Mao, but you can’t actually be a Maoist. The 2018 Jasic incident in Shenzhen made this contradiction very clear. At the time, some workers at Jasic Technology wanted to form a union, and leftist students from universities like Peking University went to support them. These students were not liberals; many truly studied Marx, Lenin, and Mao. Some carried Mao portraits; some sang the Internationale. Workers, students, Marxism, Mao Zedong—according to the. official CCP textbooks, these are all the correct answers. But what was the result? The workers were arrested, the supporters were detained, and Marxist societies in universities were suppressed. Why? Because the issue was never about whether you read Marx; it’s about who gave you permission to organize yourself. Reading the Communist Manifesto in a classroom is fine, but it’s a different story when you actually go out and organize workers. In 2021, delivery rider Chen Guojiang organized the "Meng Shou Hu" network to speak up. for riders, only to face suppression later. The real issue is that the CCP doesn't fear you studying a dead revolution; it fears you learning how to organize from it. Is Mao Zedong really the cure? Some might misunderstand me at this point. " >> Hey, are you saying that since young people in the mainland are unhappy with bureaucratic capitalism and the wealth gap, they should just go back to the Maoist path?" >> Not exactly. I actually think this is the most dangerous part of the whole " Leftist" trend. Because when a society is disillusioned with the present, it’s prone to the mistake of romanticizing a past it never personally lived through. Many young people in China see the young Mao, the crossing of the river, the Long March, the Korean War, and Nixon’s visit , all set to inspiring music. But what’s edited out of these videos? The Anti-Rightist Campaign? The Great Leap Forward? The Great Famine? What about the Cultural Revolution and the countless ordinary people whose lives. were destroyed, humiliated, and persecuted? Those are all missing. Mao did leave behind political rhetoric about opposing privilege and valuing equality. But we cannot forget that the same political system also created a country where there were virtually no institutional checks on the supreme leader. When a leader is always " correct," the media can’t criticize them , the judiciary can’t restrain them, and the people can’t vote them out, then even the noble word "people" can become.

a pretext for disaster. So, if we hope for another unchecked strongman because we're frustrated by bureaucratic capitalism, or if we romanticize tearing down the system with mass movements because current channels for dissent are blocked, that isn't liberation—it’s just using 20 th-century poison to treat 21 st-century ailments. Also, note that youth anxiety isn't unique to China. Taiwan has high housing prices and low wages; South Korea has "Hell Joseon" and the "N-po generation." Young people. everywhere are dissatisfied with corporate dominance, class rigidity, and a lack of future. Don't simplify this by pretending youth in democracies are always happy. Democracy won't drop a house from the sky or guarantee you a high salary. So, what is democracy actually good for? I believe its most important function is providing legitimate tools to use when you are dissatisfied. Unhappy with the government? Vote. Think labor treatment is unfair? Form a union. Think the ruling party is terrible? Support or. even start a new party. Want to criticize the president? Do it publicly . If you think the government broke the law, go through the judicial system. The large-scale protests in South Korea weren't as simple as people hitting the streets and the president stepping down the next day; it was civic mobilization , media investigation, parliamentary impeachment, and judicial processes all working together. This is called institutionalized political venting. The greatest value of democracy isn't the absence of social conflict, but ensuring conflict doesn't require revolution to be solved, so people don't have to wait for a savior or another messiah. So if. someone asks me if it’s terrifying that young people in mainland China are reading Mao's works, I would say I’m not actually that afraid of them reading them. History should be read, and Mao Zedong is a very important figure in modern Chinese history, so he is worth studying. What I find truly tragic is why they have so few political languages to choose from when they want to discuss politics. Can liberalism be organized openly? Can social democracy openly form a political party? Can a truly independent labor union be established? Can the media truly investigate the highest authorities? If these paths are all blocked, what is left for the youth ? What remains is a Mao Zedong that even the CCP cannot openly deny. So, in a way , today’s "Mao Fever" isn't Mao’s victory, but a price paid for political language poverty. When a 21 st-century youth has to run back to the 20th century to find language to express their labor plight, political anxiety, and social dissatisfaction, that in. itself is worth thinking about. And for Sun Yat-sen's perspective, it’s even clearer, since the CCP claims to be the successor to his revolutionary cause. So let’s actually examine it through the Three Principles of the People: Nationalism, Democracy, and Livelihood. Which one is shouted the loudest in the mainland today? Nationalism, of course. National rejuvenation, the rise of a great power, the "century of humiliation "—but I have to ask, is a country becoming strong the same thing as an ordinary young person living well? No.

You can have many aircraft carriers and the world’s second-largest GDP, but if a 25-year-old works 12 hours a day and still can't afford to marry, have children, or buy a home, what does the " rise of a great power" really have to do with their life? That’s why Sun Yat-sen talked about Livelihood—equalization of land rights and regulation of capital. The core behind it is that national development cannot just make a few people rich; ordinary people must have the chance to live a secure life. But even more important than Livelihood is Democracy. Who monitors the government? If the government does something wrong, can the people replace them? Can laborers form their own unions? Can the people stand in the way? Can journalists investigate the leadership? Can ordinary people publicly criticize the President without fear? If the answers are all no , then "people as masters of the country " eventually just means someone else is acting as master for them. True civil rights aren't the government saying "I represent you"; true civil rights are people having the power to tell the government, "You do not represent me, I. want someone else." So in the end, I believe the "Mao fever" in China today isn't really telling us that Mao Zedong has returned, but rather that young people are looking for a language to explain their situation. Some look to nationalism, some to class struggle, some to self-help, and some to Mao, but a truly modern nation shouldn't force people to keep searching for answers in the past. A healthy political system should allow an ordinary person, rather than a great. leader, to change their country. If I am unsatisfied today, I don't need a revolution; I just vote you out. If I think a company is exploiting workers, I don't need to call for a Cultural Revolution; I form a union. If I believe the government is corrupt, I don't need to wait for another Mao; I can let the media investigate, let the legislature oversee, and let the judiciary hold them accountable. That is a truly mature political system. So looking back at " Mao fever," it’s not just simple Mao worship, nor is it a sign that Chinese. youth are turning entirely to the left. It contains nationalism, populism, self-help, youth facing unemployment, and anxiety over class rigidity, as well as those using Mao—whom the CCP cannot deny—to secretly question the CCP today . What’s truly worth understanding isn't why these young people are so foolish to believe in Mao again, but why a 21 st-century youth, in order to express their pain, must run back to the 20th century to borrow the words of a dead. leader? I can understand their dissatisfaction, but understanding doesn't mean we must re-embrace the Mao era. Because what mainland China truly needs today isn't another infallible leader, but a system where people can be their own masters even without one. When ordinary people living in mainland China can freely elect their government , publicly criticize national leaders, form political parties, establish truly independent unions, enjoy freedom of.

press and belief, and speak out—when they can vote a government out if it fails, or hold officials accountable through the judiciary—then Chinese youth won't need to dig a voice out of a historical coffin to speak for them, because they will have their own. And I believe this is what true "people as masters of the country,""the world for the public," and "the people's aspiration" really mean. Striving for a China that truly realizes freedom, democracy, civil rights, and prestige remains our unchanging goal. The. politics of the National Revolution may face a hundred setbacks, but they will never end. Alright, that’s all for today’s story. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解作者如何解讀國民黨與共產黨之間的組織衝突，以及「清黨」理念的形成。
  • 認識作者對西山會議派的歷史定位，包括其反共、民族主義與文化論述。
  • 看見作者如何將歷史議題連結到當代政治，並思考政治原則與策略之間的張力。

摘要

組織滲透與清黨理念

作者認為，孫中山打破聯俄容共的合作格局後，國民黨內的思想混亂也成為針對國民黨的心理戰。他主張，反共不只是一種思想立場，也必須落實為組織原則：若一個組織遭到滲透並被他人掌控，就不再真正屬於原來的組織。作者因此將西山會議派描述為國民黨史上最早倡議整肅黨務的派別，主張清除中央執行委員會中的共產黨員，並撤銷加入國民黨的共產黨員黨籍。

西山會議派對「共產分子」的界定

作者特別指出，西山會議派的決議使用「共產分子」一詞，而非單指「共產黨」，並將其解釋為兩類人：明確信奉共產主義者，以及背離國民黨理念、轉而投向共產黨或蘇聯的原國民黨成員。作者認為，這套論述為清黨提供了理論依據；他也表示，蔣介石後來採納清黨觀念，在武漢政府受到共產黨與蘇聯影響後，於上海及全國推行清黨。

作者對清黨歷史的重新詮釋

作者反駁「蔣介石先清除共產黨人」的說法，聲稱在廖仲愷逝世後，蘇聯與共產黨勢力已先行排除國民黨內的反對者，西山會議派有二十四席中央委員中的十一席，仍遭到全數除名。依作者的說法，國民黨是在自身成員受到排擠、被逼入困境後，才開始清除共產黨人。他將這種解讀稱為歷史事實，並以此強調西山會議派在清黨思想上的先行地位。

民族主義與反對蘇聯帝國主義

作者接著提出民族主義的反共原則，並稱西山會議派最早揭示蘇聯也是一種新帝國主義勢力，認為它承襲沙皇俄國的擴張性，只是改以分化、欺騙等方式掩飾。作者引用居正的說法，主張應看穿共產主義的外衣，辨認蘇聯的帝國主義本質；他也提到，西山會議派曾致函蘇聯駐華代表加拉罕，指責蘇聯以帝國主義方式對待中國。

國家認同與當代政治的連結

值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解作者如何解讀國民黨與共產黨之間的組織衝突，以及「清黨」理念的形成。
  • 認識作者對西山會議派的歷史定位，包括其反共、民族主義與文化論述。
  • 看見作者如何將歷史議題連結到當代政治，並思考政治原則與策略之間的張力。

摘要

組織滲透與清黨理念

作者認為，孫中山打破聯俄容共的合作格局後，國民黨內的思想混亂也成為針對國民黨的心理戰。他主張，反共不只是一種思想立場，也必須落實為組織原則：若一個組織遭到滲透並被他人掌控，就不再真正屬於原來的組織。作者因此將西山會議派描述為國民黨史上最早倡議整肅黨務的派別，主張清除中央執行委員會中的共產黨員，並撤銷加入國民黨的共產黨員黨籍。

西山會議派對「共產分子」的界定

作者特別指出，西山會議派的決議使用「共產分子」一詞，而非單指「共產黨」，並將其解釋為兩類人：明確信奉共產主義者，以及背離國民黨理念、轉而投向共產黨或蘇聯的原國民黨成員。作者認為，這套論述為清黨提供了理論依據；他也表示，蔣介石後來採納清黨觀念，在武漢政府受到共產黨與蘇聯影響後，於上海及全國推行清黨。

作者對清黨歷史的重新詮釋

作者反駁「蔣介石先清除共產黨人」的說法，聲稱在廖仲愷逝世後，蘇聯與共產黨勢力已先行排除國民黨內的反對者，西山會議派有二十四席中央委員中的十一席，仍遭到全數除名。依作者的說法，國民黨是在自身成員受到排擠、被逼入困境後，才開始清除共產黨人。他將這種解讀稱為歷史事實，並以此強調西山會議派在清黨思想上的先行地位。

民族主義與反對蘇聯帝國主義

作者接著提出民族主義的反共原則，並稱西山會議派最早揭示蘇聯也是一種新帝國主義勢力，認為它承襲沙皇俄國的擴張性，只是改以分化、欺騙等方式掩飾。作者引用居正的說法，主張應看穿共產主義的外衣，辨認蘇聯的帝國主義本質；他也提到，西山會議派曾致函蘇聯駐華代表加拉罕，指責蘇聯以帝國主義方式對待中國。

國家認同與當代政治的連結

作者將反帝與民族主義連結到維護民主、領土完整及國家不被分裂，並以日本在東北扶植滿洲國為例，批評分裂國家的行為。他又把這套論述延伸至當代台灣政治，質疑部分自稱民主的人士支持台灣獨立，認為相關主張可能使台灣陷入動盪，並從中使中國共產黨得利。這些是作者對當代政治的判斷與批評。

文化反共與傳統價值

作者表示，西山會議派也提出文化層面的反共主張，並以忠、孝、仁、義、廉、和平等價值概括他所認為的中國傳統文化。他認為，共產主義企圖切斷傳統、破壞民族文化，並以自身文化取而代之；談到文化大革命時，他聲稱大量寺廟與文物遭到焚毀或破壞。因此，他主張文化反共不只是國民黨的黨內原則，也應成為中國民族的共同立場。

值得閱讀的理由

  • 了解作者如何解讀國民黨與共產黨之間的組織衝突，以及「清黨」理念的形成。
  • 認識作者對西山會議派的歷史定位，包括其反共、民族主義與文化論述。
  • 看見作者如何將歷史議題連結到當代政治，並思考政治原則與策略之間的張力。

摘要

組織滲透與清黨理念

作者認為，孫中山打破聯俄容共的合作格局後，國民黨內的思想混亂也成為針對國民黨的心理戰。他主張，反共不只是一種思想立場，也必須落實為組織原則：若一個組織遭到滲透並被他人掌控，就不再真正屬於原來的組織。作者因此將西山會議派描述為國民黨史上最早倡議整肅黨務的派別，主張清除中央執行委員會中的共產黨員，並撤銷加入國民黨的共產黨員黨籍。

西山會議派對「共產分子」的界定

作者特別指出，西山會議派的決議使用「共產分子」一詞，而非單指「共產黨」，並將其解釋為兩類人：明確信奉共產主義者，以及背離國民黨理念、轉而投向共產黨或蘇聯的原國民黨成員。作者認為，這套論述為清黨提供了理論依據；他也表示，蔣介石後來採納清黨觀念，在武漢政府受到共產黨與蘇聯影響後，於上海及全國推行清黨。
